model_note.S:
cc: Severe flank pain that comes in waves

HPI: 27 yo f. Patient reports: It started suddenly 4 hours ago. It is in my left flank. It travels toward my left groin. It is sharp and cramping in waves. At its worst it is 9/10. Each wave lasts several minutes with partial easing between. It started while I was at work, without trauma. Nothing reliably relieves it. There is no clear movement trigger. I tried acetaminophen 500 mg without relief. I had a kidney stone 5 years ago. It needed a procedure to remove it. The left flank hurts in waves. My urine looked pink once. I feel nauseated with the pain. I vomited once. The pain is exhausting.

Patient perspective: Will this damage my kidney?

PMH: One prior calcium kidney stone; has two kidneys; no kidney disease.

PSH: Ureteroscopy for stone removal at age 22; temporary stent removed 1 week later. No other operations.

Meds: No daily medicines; acetaminophen once today.

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

SH: Never smoked tobacco. Two alcoholic drinks weekly. No recreational drugs. Construction estimator; often cannot take water breaks; lives with husband.

FH: My dad is fifty-six and he's had kidney stones over and over.; My mom is fifty-four and she has high blood pressure.; I have one sister and she's healthy.

ROS: Urinary - Reports flank pain. Reports hematuria. Denies dysuria. Gastrointestinal - Reports nausea. Reports vomiting. Denies diarrhea. General - Denies fever. Denies chills. Reports fatigue.
Urinary history: I am still able to pass urine.
Reproductive history: I do not think I am pregnant, but I have not taken a pregnancy test.
Reproductive history: My last period was 2 weeks ago.
model_note.O:
Vitals: T 98.7 F oral, P 98 bpm, BP 142/86 mmHg, R 20 rpm, Pulse Ox 99% on room air, Ht 5' 7", Wt 165 lbs

General: Alert. Restless, frequently changing position.

Heart: Regular rhythm without murmur.

Lungs: Clear breath sounds bilaterally.

Abd: Abdomen not distended. Bowel sounds present. Mild left lateral abdominal tenderness. No involuntary guarding. Tympanic over examined quadrants. Left costovertebral angle tenderness; right side nontender.

Osteopathic: T10 paraspinal tissue texture change with mild tenderness on the right.

Skin: No visible rash on the inspected arms.
P: 1. Assess pain control, hydration, urine output, solitary kidney and infection risk; obtain urinalysis, creatinine and appropriate renal imaging; provide clinician-directed analgesia and antiemetic, with urgent urology for infected obstruction or renal compromise; explain urine straining if discharged and arrange a symptom and result review within 48–72 hours after acute assessment if stable for outpatient care, with emergency return for fever or inability to urinate.

2. Obtain urine culture if infection is suspected and monitor systemic features; an obstructed infected urinary system needs urgent drainage evaluation rather than antibiotics alone; explain the fever/rigor emergency precaution.

3. Ask about mechanical triggers and assess focal musculature after urgent renal causes; consider conservative treatment only if supported; advise reassessment for new urinary or systemic features. If urgent renal causes are excluded and a muscular cause is supported, advise continued gentle daily activity as tolerated and avoidance of prolonged bed rest. If a focal muscle strain is supported, consider acetaminophen after reviewing contraindications and the response to the earlier dose.

model_note.S:
cc: Severe flank pain that comes in waves

HPI: 27 yo f. Patient reports: It started suddenly 9 hours ago. It is in my left flank. It travels toward my left groin. It is sharp and cramping in waves. At its worst it is 9/10. Each wave lasts several minutes with partial easing between. It started while I was at work, without trauma. Nothing reliably relieves it. There is no clear movement trigger. I tried acetaminophen 500 mg without relief. I had a kidney stone 5 years ago. It needed a procedure to remove it. The left flank hurts in waves. My urine looked pink once. I feel nauseated with the pain. I vomited once. The pain is exhausting.

Patient perspective: Will this damage my kidney?

PMH: One prior calcium kidney stone; has two kidneys; no kidney disease.

PSH: Ureteroscopy for stone removal at age 22; temporary stent removed 1 week later. No other operations.

Meds: No daily medicines; acetaminophen once today.

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

SH: Never smoked tobacco. Two alcoholic drinks weekly. No recreational drugs. Construction estimator; often cannot take water breaks; lives with husband.

FH: My dad is fifty-six and he's had kidney stones over and over.; My mom is fifty-four and she has high blood pressure.; I have one sister and she's healthy.

ROS: Urinary - Reports flank pain. Reports hematuria. Denies dysuria. Gastrointestinal - Reports nausea. Reports vomiting. Denies diarrhea. General - Denies fever. Denies chills. Reports fatigue.
Urinary history: I am still able to pass urine.
Reproductive history: I do not think I am pregnant, but I have not taken a pregnancy test.
Reproductive history: My last period was 2 weeks ago.
model_note.O:
Vitals: T 98.7 F oral, P 98 bpm, BP 142/86 mmHg, R 20 rpm, Pulse Ox 99% on room air, Ht 5' 7", Wt 165 lbs

General: Alert. Restless, frequently changing position.

Heart: Regular rhythm without murmur.

Lungs: Clear breath sounds bilaterally.

Abd: Abdomen not distended. Bowel sounds present. Mild left lateral abdominal tenderness. No involuntary guarding. Tympanic over examined quadrants. Left costovertebral angle tenderness; right side nontender.

Osteopathic: T10 paraspinal tissue texture change with mild tenderness on the right.

Skin: No visible rash on the inspected arms.
P: 1. Assess pain control, hydration, urine output, solitary kidney and infection risk; obtain urinalysis, creatinine and appropriate renal imaging; provide clinician-directed analgesia and antiemetic, with urgent urology for infected obstruction or renal compromise; explain urine straining if discharged and arrange a symptom and result review within 48–72 hours after acute assessment if stable for outpatient care, with emergency return for fever or inability to urinate.

2. Obtain urine culture if infection is suspected and monitor systemic features; an obstructed infected urinary system needs urgent drainage evaluation rather than antibiotics alone; explain the fever/rigor emergency precaution.

3. Ask about mechanical triggers and assess focal musculature after urgent renal causes; consider conservative treatment only if supported; advise reassessment for new urinary or systemic features. If urgent renal causes are excluded and a muscular cause is supported, advise continued gentle daily activity as tolerated and avoidance of prolonged bed rest. If a focal muscle strain is supported, consider acetaminophen after reviewing contraindications and the response to the earlier dose.

model_note.S:
cc: Severe flank pain that comes in waves

HPI: 27 yo f. Patient reports: It started suddenly 4 hours ago. It is in my left flank. It travels toward my left groin. It is sharp and cramping in waves. At its worst it is 9/10. Each wave lasts several minutes with partial easing between. It started while I was at work, without trauma. Nothing reliably relieves it. There is no clear movement trigger. I tried acetaminophen 500 mg without relief. I had a kidney stone 5 years ago. It needed a procedure to remove it. The left flank hurts in waves. My urine looked pink once. I feel nauseated with the pain. I vomited once. The pain is exhausting.

Patient perspective: Will this damage my kidney?

PMH: One prior calcium kidney stone; has two kidneys; no kidney disease.

PSH: Ureteroscopy for stone removal at age 22; temporary stent removed 1 week later. No other operations.

Meds: No daily medicines; acetaminophen once today.

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

SH: Never smoked tobacco. Two alcoholic drinks weekly. No recreational drugs. Construction estimator; often cannot take water breaks; lives with husband.

FH: My dad is fifty-six and he's had kidney stones over and over.; My mom is fifty-four and she has high blood pressure.; I have one sister and she's healthy.

ROS: Urinary - Reports flank pain. Reports hematuria. Denies dysuria. Gastrointestinal - Reports nausea. Reports vomiting. Denies diarrhea. General - Denies fever. Denies chills. Reports fatigue.

P: 1. Assess pain control, hydration, urine output, solitary kidney and infection risk; obtain urinalysis, creatinine and appropriate renal imaging; provide clinician-directed analgesia and antiemetic, with urgent urology for infected obstruction or renal compromise; explain urine straining if discharged and arrange a symptom and result review within 48–72 hours after acute assessment if stable for outpatient care, with emergency return for fever or inability to urinate. Discuss a concrete follow-up route and work documentation while explaining which warning signs cannot wait.

2. Obtain urine culture if infection is suspected and monitor systemic features; an obstructed infected urinary system needs urgent drainage evaluation rather than antibiotics alone; explain the fever/rigor emergency precaution.

3. Ask about mechanical triggers and assess focal musculature after urgent renal causes; consider conservative treatment only if supported; advise reassessment for new urinary or systemic features. If urgent renal causes are excluded and a muscular cause is supported, advise continued gentle daily activity as tolerated and avoidance of prolonged bed rest. If a focal muscle strain is supported, consider acetaminophen after reviewing contraindications and the response to the earlier dose.
